extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards about wartime news reporting from Moscow and other fronts during World War II — how correspondent dispatches are produced, censored, and evaluated for reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary sources for Soviet war news
rubrics_metrics.description: The sources of information are exceptionally trustworthy. They are the Soviet press, official communiques and eyewitness observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The single greatest source is the newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda, or Red Star, official organ of the Commissariat of Defense. Correspondents combine Soviet press material, official communiques and on-site eyewitness visits in their reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and distribution of communiques
rubrics_metrics.description: The communiques are issued each noon and night. Copies are handed to foreign correspondents at about the same time they are delivered into Soviet news offices and broadcast by Moscow radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communiques typically list points recaptured and give details on individual operations; they form the backbone of war reporting from Moscow and are used as a reference against which correspondent dispatches are compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted content under Soviet censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The censors watch for information which might aid or give comfort to the enemy, and also for any that might be misleading or incorrect in their opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any article which seems to the censors a reasonable interpretation of the facts given by the Soviet press or communique, or witnessed at the front, is permitted to pass. Censorship was once the strictest but has become more liberal; correspondents sometimes were limited entirely to what appeared in the Soviet press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondent access and observational limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign correspondents are permitted on the front only after the Red army has won a victory and consolidated its new positions; they do not see actual combat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although they do not witness fighting, correspondents can inspect the scenes of battle and interview officers and men who participated, and they sometimes make group visits to the front to verify reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and typical limitations of Moscow dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: The correspondents are substantially reliable. They do not always tell the whole story, and the figures may sometimes be out of line, but in general what they say is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures on enemy casualties were sometimes overestimated early in the war; now, with more opportunity to confirm estimates as Russians advance, correspondents consider figures more reliable. There is no known case in Moscow correspondents' experience of a false Soviet claim to capture of any point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official handling of contradictory battlefield outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When German counter-attacks have resulted in recapture of points the Soviet authorities do not make misleading statements about such action, but usually lapse into silence on that operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such silences are understood by the Russian people and reflect an official practice of avoiding misleading claims rather than issuing corrections; reporters and readers should interpret omissions in that context.
